subsection: 10. Cultural revivals and the consolidation of Catholic identity

notes.h: Background and key terms: why a cultural revival, and why Catholic identity
notes.b: By the 1880s many Irish people felt that politics alone had not made Ireland distinct, and that the country's own culture was fading. Below are the background events and the vocabulary that the rest of the subsection depends on.
points: The Great Famine (1845–52) killed about one million people and led to the emigration of about one million more. Irish as a spoken language fell sharply after the Famine.
English was the language of the state, law and commerce, and the national school system (begun in 1831) taught in English. Revivalists later set out to restore Irish.
Anglicisation means adopting English language, dress, games, names and manners. De-anglicisation is Douglas Hyde's programme to reverse this by reviving the Irish language, games, music and customs.

The Anglo-Irish were the mainly Protestant landowning and professional class with English ties, many of them unionist (supporters of the union with Britain). In this subsection the term also labels the writers of the Literary Revival, and is the label their critics used for them.

Cultural nationalism defines the nation by its language, culture and tradition rather than by parliaments and votes. The Gaelic League, the GAA and the Literary Revival were all cultural nationalist movements.
Irish Ireland is D.P. Moran's idea of a Gaelic and Catholic nation built on the Irish language, Irish industry and Irish games. It was narrower than Hyde's approach.

The Catholic Church under Paul Cullen (archbishop of Armagh from 1849 and of Dublin from 1852, with the Synod of Thurles in 1850) set about reforming Irish Catholic practice. The Catholic majority also gave nationalist politics (the Home Rule movement and Parnell) its weight.
The GAA, founded at Thurles on 1 November 1884, was the first of the cultural bodies. There is more on this in the notes on the GAA to 1891.
notes.tip: Exams on cultural and religious identity expect you to link the Catholic strand, the Gaelic strand and the Anglo-Irish strand. Keep these terms clear so you can use them precisely.

notes.h: Douglas Hyde and the de-anglicisation argument (1892)
notes.b: Hyde's lecture of 1892 gave the cultural revival its programme: Irish people should stop imitating England and revive their own language and customs.
points: Douglas Hyde delivered The Necessity for De-Anglicising Ireland to the National Literary Society in Dublin on 25 November 1892. The Society had been founded in Dublin that year, with Hyde, Yeats and John O'Leary among those involved.

Hyde argued that Ireland had been anglicised in language, names, dress, music, games and ideas. The Irish, he said, were neither fully English nor fully Irish, because they had abandoned their own ways without becoming truly English.
He urged the revival of Irish and of native customs, so that Ireland could preserve what was distinctive about it rather than copy England.

The lecture was presented as non-political: its aim was cultural, and it appealed to all creeds and parties. This is why it could later support a League that welcomed Catholics, Protestants, nationalists and unionists.
Hyde pointed to the decline of Irish as a spoken language, which had fallen sharply since the Famine, and asked for it to be cultivated and used in schools.
The GAA (1884) had already shown the appeal of native games. The lecture gave a wider programme, covering language and customs, and led within a year to the founding of the Gaelic League.
notes.tip: Do not mix up the dates: the lecture was 1892 (to the National Literary Society) and the Gaelic League was founded in 1893.

notes.b: The Gaelic League, founded in 1893, turned Hyde's argument into a mass movement to revive the Irish language. Its story is one of real successes, then growing political pressure.
points: The Gaelic League (Conradh na Gaeilge) was founded in Dublin on 31 July 1893 by Douglas Hyde, Eoin MacNeill and others, with Hyde as president.
It was officially non-political and non-sectarian, so it welcomed Catholics, Protestants, nationalists and unionists. This broad stance helped it recruit across the divisions of Irish society.
Branches ran Irish classes, so that adults could learn the language, and timirí (travelling teachers of Irish) were sent to rural areas. There were several hundred branches by the mid-1900s.

The League organised feiseanna (festivals of music, dance and language competitions), so that people could enjoy Irish culture and not only study it, and, from 1897, the annual festival called the Oireachtas.
Its weekly paper An Claidheamh Soluis began in 1899, and Patrick Pearse edited it from 1903 to 1909. This gave the League a way to spread its ideas.
Success in schools: Irish was admitted to primary schools as an ordinary subject by the Revised Programme of 1900, and a bilingual programme followed in 1904.

Success at university: the League won a campaign to make Irish compulsory for matriculation (the entrance qualification) to the National University of Ireland. The Senate decided this in 1910 and it applied from 1913.
Language processions on St Patrick's Day began in 1903, the year it became a bank holiday in Ireland. People also took Irish names and used Irish-language signs.
notes.tip: For a short account of the League, give the founding date, the founders, the non-political stance, the activities (classes, feiseanna, timirí, paper) and the achievements, each as a separate dated statement.

notes.h: The Gaelic League: who joined, politicisation and limits
notes.b: The League drew on a wide social range, but the same success that made it influential also pulled it into politics and exposed its limits.
points: The League's membership included women, teachers and the urban middle class, and its leadership was based in Dublin. This differed from the GAA, which was rural and male.
From about 1910 a growing number of IRB members (the Irish Republican Brotherhood, a secret society that wanted an independent republic) joined the League. They pushed it towards politics.

Hyde resigned as president in 1915 after the League's Ard Fheis (annual convention) in July 1915 adopted a political aim. This is later context: it shows that the League's non-political stance did not survive.
Limit: Irish did not revive as an everyday language, so the main aim was not reached, even though the League put it into schools and the university.

Limit: the Church's support was limited. Fr Michael O'Hickey, professor of Irish at Maynooth, was dismissed in 1909 by the bishops (the college trustees) after campaigning for compulsory Irish in the National University.
notes.tip: If asked about the League's politicisation, name the cause (IRB members joining from about 1910), the person (Pearse is linked to this) and the result (Hyde's resignation in 1915).

notes.b: Hyde was the scholar who launched the language revival and gave it a non-sectarian, non-political character. He was both a founder of the movement and, in the end, a man overtaken by it.
points: Douglas Hyde (1860–1949) was born in Castlerea, Co. Roscommon, the son of a Church of Ireland rector. He learned Irish from the people around him in Frenchpark and studied at Trinity College Dublin.

He published collections of Gaelic songs and folktales, including Love Songs of Connacht (1893), and wrote under the pen name An Craoibhín Aoibhinn (the little branch of delight). His Irish-language play Casadh an tSúgáin was staged in 1901.
He was a participant: he gave the 1892 lecture, co-founded the League in 1893 and led it as president for twenty-two years, until 1915.
He was shaped by events: the League's politicisation after about 1910 overtook his non-political aim, and he resigned as president in 1915 when it adopted a political aim.

Contemporaries admired his scholarship and his appeal across religious lines. Irish Irelanders disliked the League's non-political, non-sectarian stance, and republicans criticised him later as the League turned political.
He later became a senator (1925) and the first President of Ireland (1938–45), and died in 1949.
Historians credit him with launching the revival and a mass interest in the language, while recognising that its later political use went beyond his intentions.
notes.tip: Profiles of Hyde earn marks for dated, correct statements: birth and background, the 1892 lecture, the 1893 League, the 1915 resignation, and his presidency. Both Hyde and Yeats were Protestants outside the Catholic majority, which is a useful point of comparison.

notes.b: Moran gave the revival a sharper edge by defining the Irish nation as Gaelic and Catholic. His view challenged Hyde's inclusive approach.
points: David Patrick Moran founded the weekly newspaper The Leader in 1900 and used it to argue for an Irish Ireland.
He urged support for Irish language, industry and games, and attacked the Anglo-Irish literary movement and the Irish Party as West Britons, his term for Irish people who imitated English ways.
In his view the nation was Gaelic and Catholic, so Protestants could be accepted only if they adopted this identity.
His book The Philosophy of Irish Ireland (1905) collected his articles and set out his creed.
The Leader promoted boycotts of English goods and entertainment, to support Irish industry, and attacked music-hall and English newspapers.
Moran's influence divided the revival between Hyde's inclusive approach and a narrower Catholic and Gaelic nationalism.
notes.tip: Contrast Moran's exclusive Irish Ireland with the League's official non-sectarian stance under Hyde.

notes.b: A group of mainly Protestant writers in English drew on Irish myth, folklore and peasant speech to create a national literature and theatre. Unlike the League, they wrote in English, which is why Irish Irelanders distrusted them.
points: The National Literary Society was founded in Dublin in 1892, with Hyde and Yeats among its leaders.

The Irish Literary Theatre was founded in 1899 by W.B. Yeats, Lady Gregory and Edward Martyn. Its first production, in May 1899, was Yeats's The Countess Cathleen. In 1901 it staged Hyde's Irish-language play Casadh an tSúgáin.
Cathleen ni Houlihan, credited to Yeats with Lady Gregory's help, was first staged on 2 April 1902, with Maud Gonne (a nationalist activist) in the title role. It was a nationalist play.
The Abbey Theatre opened on 27 December 1904, funded by the English patron Annie Horniman, with Yeats, Lady Gregory and J.M. Synge as directors.
Lady Gregory (1852–1932), for example, was an Anglo-Irish landowner from Coole Park, Co. Galway. She wrote plays, collected folklore, and acted as patron and organiser of the Abbey as a director.
John Millington Synge (1871–1909) drew on the speech of the Aran Islands and the west of Ireland. His The Playboy of the Western World was first performed at the Abbey in January 1907.
notes.tip: Keep the three bodies in order: National Literary Society (1892), Irish Literary Theatre (1899) and Abbey Theatre (1904). Do not confuse Cathleen ni Houlihan (1902, a nationalist play) with The Countess Cathleen (1899, a controversy over heresy).

notes.b: Yeats, a Protestant poet and dramatist, tried to give Ireland a literature that would shape a national identity. He found that the nationalists he wrote for did not always accept him.
points: William Butler Yeats (1865–1939) was born in Sandymount, Dublin, on 13 June 1865, the son of the painter John Butler Yeats. He spent much of his childhood in Sligo and London, and was a Protestant.

His early poetry, such as The Wanderings of Oisin (1889), drew on Irish mythology. His friendship with the nationalist activist Maud Gonne and with John O'Leary, the old Fenian who influenced him, linked him to political circles.
He was a participant who co-founded the National Literary Society, the Irish Literary Theatre and the Abbey (as a director), and was linked to the play Cathleen ni Houlihan.
He was shaped by events, so his views changed: the Countess Cathleen and Playboy controversies and the Lane dispute pushed him towards a critique of nationalist Ireland.

September 1913, published in the Irish Times on 8 September 1913, followed the Hugh Lane dispute. It condemned the narrow Catholic middle class for lacking the generosity of earlier Irish rebels, and its refrain is: Romantic Ireland's dead and gone.

Contemporary nationalists admired his work but distrusted his Anglo-Irish background, because he was a Protestant writing in English. Moran mocked him, and Catholic critics attacked The Countess Cathleen.
He later served as a senator (1922–28), won the Nobel Prize in Literature in 1923, and died in 1939.
Historians such as R.F. Foster (W.B. Yeats: A Life, volume 1 in 1997 and volume 2 in 2003) see him at the centre of Irish cultural life, while critics find an elitist streak in his politics.
notes.tip: Hyde and Yeats are often asked as a pair. Give what each did (Hyde: lecture and League; Yeats: Literary Theatre and Abbey), their backgrounds with dates, and how far each shaped Irish identity.

notes.b: The revival was marked by public disputes about who defined Irish identity. Each controversy shows the clash between the Anglo-Irish and Irish Ireland visions.
points: The Countess Cathleen (1899) was attacked as heretical by Catholic critics. Frank Hugh O'Donnell's pamphlet Souls for Gold (1899) was a leading attack.

The Playboy riots of January 1907 followed because nationalist audiences objected to the play's picture of rural Irish people. They showed the clash between the Abbey's artistic freedom and the nationalist demand for flattering images of Irish life.

The Hugh Lane dispute began when Sir Hugh Lane offered his collection of French paintings to Dublin and Dublin Corporation hesitated over funding and a site for a gallery (1912–13). Lane withdrew the offer and lent the pictures to the National Gallery in London in 1913.

Lane died on the Lusitania on 7 May 1915. An unwitnessed codicil (an addition to his will) left the pictures to Dublin, leading to a long dispute that was only settled by a shared arrangement in 1959.
Nationalists argued that Irish culture should be Gaelic and Catholic, while the Anglo-Irish writers claimed a place for English-language literature and for Protestant traditions.
Tension between the two visions, Anglo-Irish and Irish Ireland, ran through the revival and remained after independence.
notes.tip: When asked who objected and why, name the objectors (Catholic critics for Countess Cathleen; nationalist audiences for Playboy), state the objection, and say what it showed about the two visions. Note that Dublin Corporation hesitated; it did not refuse. Give only January 1907 for the Playboy.

notes.h: The devotional revolution and the Church's reach
notes.b: After the Famine the Catholic Church tightened its hold on Irish life. Its influence grew through worship, buildings, schools and the clergy.
points: Historians speak of a devotional revolution, a term coined by the historian Emmet Larkin (1972) for the post-Famine rise in Mass attendance and devotional practice under Cullen. From the 1850s there were parish missions, retreats, confraternities and devotions such as the Rosary and the Sacred Heart.
New churches and cathedrals were built across the country, which made the Church's presence visible, funded by a more prosperous farming and trading middle class.

The Church controlled most national schools through clerical managers (priests who ran the schools). It ran secondary schools through religious orders such as the Christian Brothers, Jesuits and convent teaching orders, so it shaped what young Catholics learned.

St Patrick's College, Maynooth, trained a large clergy, which held a high social position in rural communities. Priests were often involved in politics, and individual priests were active in local GAA clubs.
Sodalities and confraternities (lay associations for prayer and devotion) organised lay devotion, so ordinary parishioners, not only priests, took part in religious life.
The Pioneer Total Abstinence Association was founded in 1898 by Fr James Cullen, a Jesuit, to fight drunkenness.
notes.tip: Do not confuse Fr James Cullen SJ (the Pioneers) with Paul Cullen (the archbishop linked to the devotional revolution).

notes.h: How Catholic and nationalist identity merged, and the unionist reaction
notes.b: From the 1880s Catholic identity and nationalist identity increasingly overlapped, and unionists reacted with fear. This was one of the main results of the Church's growing role.
points: The Ne Temere decree, in force from Easter 1908, declared that marriages not before a Catholic priest were invalid for Catholics and required the children of mixed marriages to be raised as Catholics. This angered Protestants.
The land reforms and expanding education produced a Catholic middle class, which provided the personnel of the nationalist movement.
The Catholic bishops generally supported Home Rule from 1885, which tied Catholic identity to nationalism. The Irish Party was largely Catholic.

Unionists reacted by presenting Home Rule as Rome Rule, their slogan. The Church's role in the Parnell split (the hierarchy condemned Parnell in December 1890 after the divorce scandal) and Ne Temere reinforced the fear. There is more on this in the notes on unionism and the Ulster question.
notes.tip: For a question on cultural and religious identity, link the devotional revolution, school control and Ne Temere to a Catholic and nationalist identity, then balance it with the Gaelic and Anglo-Irish strands and the unionist reaction. Do not confuse Ne Temere (1908, mixed marriages) with the Parnell split (1890).

notes.h: The GAA after 1891 and comparison with the Gaelic League
notes.b: The GAA recovered in the 1890s and the two bodies became partners and rivals. Comparing them is a favourite exam task.
points: The GAA was weakened by the Parnell split and the crisis of 1891 and recovered slowly through the 1890s, when clubs were reorganised and competitions resumed.
The IRB remained influential in its leadership. The GAA also banned its members from playing foreign games, a rule formalised in the early 1900s.
It bought grounds at Jones's Road in Dublin in 1908; the ground was later called Croke Park.
The GAA was mass, rural, male and sport-based. The League drew women, teachers and the urban middle class, and its work was language and education.
The GAA was politically committed from the start, whereas the League was non-political until 1915.
Both were created by cultural nationalists and shared the aim of de-anglicisation and many members. Key names differ: Michael Cusack and Maurice Davin for the GAA, Hyde and MacNeill for the League.
notes.tip: In a comparison essay, give one paragraph for each body with dates and named people, then compare them: mass versus language, non-political versus political, and Catholic and Gaelic versus Anglo-Irish.

notes.h: Assessment: the revival and Catholic identity
notes.b: The revival gave Ireland a cultural identity but left argument about who belonged to it.
points: Achievement: the League, GAA and theatre created lasting institutions and symbols, and gave self-confidence to the nationalist movement.
Limit: the language did not revive as an everyday tongue, and the Catholic and Gaelic emphasis excluded many Protestants and unionists.
Contemporary unionists saw the revival as a disguise for separatism, whereas Irish Irelanders such as Moran saw the Literary Revival as too Anglo-Irish.
Historians differ on whether the revival caused the revolution of 1916, as Pearse and the IRB claimed, or merely provided a language for politics that had other causes.
notes.tip: Examiners reward achievement set against limits: the language did not revive, but the institutions and the confidence did. Naming a historian's view adds weight.

keyTerms.definition: The adoption of English language, dress, games and manners in Ireland, which the revivals set out to reverse.
The reversal of anglicisation, as proposed by Douglas Hyde in 1892, through the revival of Irish language, games and customs.
D.P. Moran’s idea that the nation should be Gaelic and Catholic, built on Irish language, industry and games.
The mainly Protestant landed and professional class with English ties, many of whose writers led the Literary Revival.
The Conradh na Gaeilge, founded in 1893 to revive the Irish language through classes, festivals and publications.
The movement of Yeats, Lady Gregory, Synge and others that drew on Irish myth and speech to create a national literature and theatre.
The national theatre opened in Dublin in December 1904, which staged the plays of the revival.
The post-Famine growth in Catholic practice, church building and organisations that strengthened Catholic identity.
The 1908 papal decree requiring the children of mixed marriages to be raised as Catholics.
The Gaelic League’s travelling teachers, who set up Irish classes in rural districts.
